definition: A specialized program that runs on the GPU to calculate rendering effects, transformations, and pixel coloring.
example: We wrote a custom compute shader to simulate water ripples efficiently in real time.

definition: A command issued by the CPU to the GPU to render a specific group of primitives.
example: Batching static meshes significantly reduced our draw calls from 1200 to under 300 per frame.

definition: A rendering technique that draws multiple copies of the same mesh simultaneously using a single draw call.
example: Enabling GPU instancing allowed us to render thousands of dynamic grass blades without CPU bottlenecking.

definition: A technique that decreases geometric complexity for 3D models as they move farther from the camera.
example: Configuring aggressive LOD transitions helped maintain a steady 60 FPS in dense open-world environments.

definition: The process of discarding objects that fall outside the camera viewing pyramid before rasterization.
example: The engine performs frustum culling automatically to avoid submitting out-of-frame geometry to the pipeline.

definition: Disabling the rendering of objects that are obscured by other opaque objects in front of them.
example: Baking occlusion culling data was essential for optimizing indoor corridor scenes with heavy architectural occluders.

definition: Pre-calculating optimized sequences of downscaled textures to improve rendering speed and eliminate aliasing artifacts.
example: Without mipmaps, distant high-frequency textures produce noticeable moiré patterns and shimmer during camera motion.

definition: The maximum time allocated per frame (e.g., 16.6ms for 60 FPS or 11.1ms for 90 FPS) to maintain target refresh rate.
example: The post-processing pass exceeded our 16.6ms frame budget, requiring downsampling of the bloom buffer.

definition: The task of converting vector graphics or 3D primitives into a raster image (pixels or dots) for display.
example: The hardware rasterizer interpolates vertex attributes across triangle fragments to feed the pixel shader.

definition: A rendering technique where lighting computations are deferred to a second pass operating on a geometric buffer (G-buffer).
example: Deferred shading decouples scene complexity from light count, allowing dozens of dynamic point lights at minimal cost.

definition: A standard rendering pipeline where each object is shaded completely in a single pass for every light affecting it.
example: We chose forward rendering with MSAA support because our VR target platform demanded low memory bandwidth.

definition: A shading methodology that models the physical behavior of light interacting with surfaces accurately.
example: Standardizing our asset pipeline around metallic-roughness PBR workflows ensured consistent look under all lighting conditions.

definition: An algorithm that traces the physical paths of light rays as they interact with virtual optical surfaces.
example: Real-time ray tracing provides physically accurate global illumination and contact reflections at high computational cost.

definition: Software and hardware techniques used to minimize jagged edges and spatial distortion in computer-rendered images.
example: Switching from FXAA to Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) eliminated geometric crawl at the cost of slight motion blur.

definition: The process of mapping high dynamic range (HDR) color values into a lower dynamic range suitable for display monitors.
example: The ACES tone mapping curve preserves highlight details without clipping bright specular reflections.

definition: A 2D buffer storing depth information for each pixel to ensure correct front-to-back geometric occlusion.
example: Z-fighting occurs when two coplanar surfaces have nearly identical values in the depth buffer.

definition: An auxiliary buffer used alongside the depth buffer to mask out specific pixels and control rendering flow.
example: We utilized the stencil buffer to render portal views and outline selected game entities.

definition: An optimization that skips rendering geometric triangles whose surface normal faces away from the camera.
example: Enabling backface culling instantly halved the number of processed fragments for closed solid meshes.

definition: A texture technique that fakes fine surface bumps and indentations by perturbing surface normals during lighting calculation.
example: Normal maps allow low-poly game models to appear intricately sculpted without inflating vertex count.

definition: A shader stage executed on the GPU outside of the standard graphics rendering pipeline for general-purpose parallel computing.
example: Flock simulation and particle physics are calculated entirely inside asynchronous compute shaders.

definition: A block of GPU memory holding vertex attribute data (positions, normals, UVs, tangents) for geometry rendering.
example: Interleaved vertex buffer layouts improve cache locality when transferring vertex data to the graphics pipeline.

definition: A buffer array containing pointers to vertex indices, allowing vertices to be reused across adjacent triangles.
example: Using an index buffer reduced mesh memory footprint by over 60% compared to raw unindexed triangle lists.

definition: A graphics pipeline stage that dynamically subdivides coarse polygons into finer geometry on the GPU.
example: Distance-based tessellation creates detailed terrain displacement near the player while conserving memory far away.

definition: Partitioning the camera frustum into multiple depth zones, each mapped to a separate shadow map resolution.
example: Cascaded Shadow Maps provide crisp close-up contact shadows while maintaining performance for horizon vistas.

definition: A technique that calculates mirror reflections by ray marching across depth and color buffers in screen space.
example: SSR creates realistic glossy reflections on wet floors but fails when reflective objects are occluded off-screen.

definition: A shading method that calculates how exposed each point in a scene is to ambient environmental lighting.
example: Screen Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO) adds soft contact shadows in crevices and corners where surfaces meet.

definition: A post-processing artifact that produces fringes of light extending from the borders of bright areas in an image.
example: Setting a proper HDR luminance threshold prevents bloom from washing out entire lit indoor rooms.

definition: A display feature that synchronizes the frame rate of the GPU with the refresh rate of the monitor to prevent screen tearing.
example: Disabling V-Sync reduced input latency for competitive players at the expense of occasional horizontal screen tearing.

definition: A visual artifact where a display device shows information from multiple frames in a single screen draw.
example: Screen tearing became prominent because the GPU was pushing frames faster than the 60Hz panel refresh cycle.

definition: The situation where the same pixel is rendered multiple times within a single frame due to overlapping geometry.
example: High particle density in alpha-blended smoke caused severe overdraw and dragged GPU fillrate down.

definition: The rate at which a graphics processing unit can render pixels or fragments to memory buffers.
example: Mobile devices are heavily fillrate-limited, making full-screen transparent post-effects prohibitively expensive.

definition: The mathematical process of combining a translucent foreground color with a background color to yield transparency.
example: Alpha blending requires sorting transparent objects back-to-front to avoid depth sorting artifacts.

definition: A reusable asset template in Unity that stores a complete GameObject with all components and property values.
example: Modifying the master enemy prefab propagates behavior changes to all instances across every game scene.

definition: A node inside an animation state machine used for smoothly blending multiple related animation clips based on input parameters.
example: We configured a 2D Freeform Directional Blend Tree to interpolate between walking, strafing, and sprinting animations.

definition: A spatial data structure that defines the walkable surfaces of a 3D environment for AI pathfinding.
example: The AI agent queries the baked NavMesh to calculate the shortest path around static physical obstacles.

definition: The process of creating a skeletal structure of bones and joints to control 3D character deformation.
example: Proper finger rigging was crucial for realistic hand poses and weapon manipulation in first-person view.

definition: Binding a 3D mesh to an underlying skeleton by assigning influence weights per vertex to each bone.
example: Smooth skinning weights around the shoulder joint prevented unsightly mesh pinching during overhead reaches.

definition: A procedural animation method that calculates joint rotations from the desired position of an end-effector (such as a foot or hand).
example: Two-bone IK dynamically aligns character feet with uneven terrain slopes to prevent floating.

definition: Projecting an invisible straight ray from a 3D origin point along a vector to detect intersecting colliders.
example: Weapon hit detection casts a physics raycast from the gun muzzle to register exact bullet impact points.

definition: A shape component that defines the physical boundary of a GameObject for collision detection.
example: Using compound primitive colliders rather than complex mesh colliders improved physics evaluation speed tenfold.

definition: A physics component that enables a GameObject to act under the control of physics forces, gravity, and mass.
example: Setting the Rigidbody interpolation to Interpolate eliminated visual stutter when moving fast objects.

definition: A frame-rate independent MonoBehaviour lifecycle method called at discrete, regular intervals for physics simulation.
example: All velocity modifications and torque applications must occur inside FixedUpdate rather than Update.

definition: A data container in Unity used to store large amounts of shared, independent data outside of scene instances.
example: Item attributes and weapon balancing numbers are stored in modular ScriptableObject assets for easy designer tuning.

definition: A method that can pause its execution and yield control back to Unity before resuming on subsequent frames.
example: We implemented a coroutine to handle the smooth fade-to-black sequence over a duration of two seconds.

definition: A Unity asset management system that makes it easy to load, build, and deploy assets asynchronously by address.
example: Migrating level textures to Addressables enabled dynamic remote content delivery and reduced the initial APK download size.

definition: An archive file containing platform-specific non-code assets that Unity can load at run-time.
example: Seasonal character skins are packaged into compressed Asset Bundles and downloaded on demand.

definition: A multithreaded architecture that lets developers write safe, performant parallel code utilizing all available CPU cores.
example: Moving our pathfinding broadphase into the C# Job System boosted processing speed by four times.

definition: An LLVM-based compiler backend that transforms Unity C# Jobs and math code into highly optimized native machine instructions.
example: Enabling the Burst Compiler vectorized our vector math operations, drastically lowering per-frame calculation times.

definition: A modular architecture consisting of ECS, the C# Job System, and the Burst Compiler designed for high performance.
example: Architecting the massive RTS simulation using DOTS allowed rendering ten thousand simultaneous units without lag.

definition: A software architectural pattern that separates data (Components) from logic (Systems) operating on unique IDs (Entities).
example: ECS avoids object-oriented overhead and cache misses by storing component data contiguously in memory chunks.

definition: Pre-calculating static direct and indirect lighting information into texture maps overlaid on scene geometry.
example: Baking high-resolution lightmaps gave our architectural walkthrough photorealistic global illumination at 60 FPS.

definition: A component that simulates and renders numerous small, moving 2D/3D images to create chaotic effects like fire, smoke, and sparks.
example: The explosion effect employs sub-emitters in the particle system to generate secondary trailing shrapnel.

definition: Simulating the acoustic properties and directional orientation of sound sources relative to the listener in 3D space.
example: Enabling binaural audio spatialization allowed players to pinpoint enemy footsteps behind walls accurately.

definition: An analysis tool that records execution timing, memory allocations, rendering bottlenecks, and audio overhead.
example: Profiling the garbage collection spikes revealed repeated string concatenations in our health bar UI loop.

definition: A UI component that controls the overall scale and pixel density of UI elements across varying screen resolutions.
example: Setting the Canvas Scaler to Scale With Screen Size ensured our HUD looks identical on phones, tablets, and 4K monitors.

definition: A component that takes geometry from the Mesh Filter and renders it at the position defined by the Transform.
example: Disabling the Mesh Renderer hides the object visually while leaving its attached collider active for triggers.

definition: The process of flattening a 3D model surface into 2D coordinates (U and V) for texture mapping.
example: Proper UV unwrapping minimizes texture stretching and optimizes UV island packing space.

definition: Specific child transform nodes linked to character bones used to attach equipment, weapons, and accessories.
example: The sword was parented to the RightHandSocket transform to follow wrist rotation during attack swings.

definition: A script attached to an Animator state that hooks into enter, update, and exit lifecycle callbacks.
example: We used a StateMachineBehaviour script to disable player movement input during the heavy landing recovery animation.

definition: Applying the position and rotation translation stored in an animation clip directly to the GameObject Transform.
example: Enabling Root Motion ensured that the character movement speed matched the visual stride of the run animation.

definition: The automatic process of converting C# data structures and object states into a format Unity can store and reload.
example: Custom structs must be decorated with [System.Serializable] to expose their fields in the Unity Inspector.

definition: The automatic memory management process that frees memory on the managed heap that is no longer referenced.
example: Eliminating LINQ allocations inside the gameplay loop avoided GC hitches that were dropping frames.

definition: A component that can be opened or closed dynamically at runtime to control occlusion culling through doors and windows.
example: Closing the occlusion portal when the dungeon door shut immediately culled the entire adjoining chamber.

definition: A 6-sided cube or panoramic sphere wrapped around the scene to simulate distant backgrounds, horizons, and ambient sky lighting.
example: A custom HDR skybox was plugged into the environment settings to drive reflection probes across shiny car surfaces.

definition: The process where client-side JavaScript attaches event listeners and state to server-rendered static HTML markup.
example: Partial hydration frameworks reduce Time to Interactive by only hydrating interactive components on the page.

definition: Rendering web pages on the server upon each client request before sending fully constructed HTML to the browser.
example: Implementing SSR improved our search engine indexing and delivered faster First Contentful Paint times.

definition: Pre-rendering web pages into static HTML, CSS, and JS files during the build phase ahead of client requests.
example: Our documentation portal uses SSG to serve lightning-fast pages directly from global CDN edge servers.

definition: A hybrid rendering mechanism that updates static pages in the background as new requests arrive without rebuilding the entire site.
example: With ISR configured at a 60-second revalidation interval, e-commerce catalog prices stay fresh without bogging down servers.

definition: Dead-code elimination performed by modern module bundlers by statically analyzing ES6 module imports and exports.
example: Tree shaking stripped out unused utility functions from Lodash, reducing our production bundle size by 45KB.

definition: Splitting application code into separate bundles loaded dynamically on demand when specific routes or components are requested.
example: Dynamic imports with React.lazy allowed us to code-split the heavy analytics dashboard from the main landing page.

definition: An in-memory representation of real DOM elements used by UI libraries to compute minimal visual update differences.
example: The virtual DOM compares previous and next states during reconciliation to batch DOM mutations efficiently.

definition: The recursive algorithm used by frameworks to diff two virtual DOM trees and determine which real DOM parts must change.
example: Providing unique key props to list items prevents the reconciliation engine from re-rendering the entire list.

definition: An optimization technique that caches the return values of expensive function calls corresponding to given inputs.
example: Wrapping complex filtering operations in useMemo avoided recomputations on unrelated component state changes.

definition: Occurs when JavaScript repeatedly writes and reads to the DOM, forcing the browser to recalculate layouts synchronously.
example: Reading element offsetHeight immediately after modifying class styles triggered severe layout thrashing and dropped frames.

definition: The sequence of steps the browser takes from receiving HTML, CSS, and JS to painting actual pixels on the screen.
example: Inlining critical CSS and deferring non-essential scripts unblocked the Critical Rendering Path.

definition: Reflow recalculates geometric positions and dimensions of elements; Repaint redraws pixel buffers without altering geometry.
example: Modifying transform and opacity properties triggers only compositing, bypassing costly reflow and repaint passes.

definition: The runtime mechanism in JavaScript that constantly coordinates task queues, microtasks, and the execution call stack.
example: Understanding the event loop is crucial to explain why Promise microtasks resolve prior to setTimeout callbacks.

definition: A prioritized queue in the event loop reserved for Promise resolutions, queueMicrotask, and MutationObserver callbacks.
example: Microtasks are processed completely until the queue is empty before the browser yields to the next rendering frame.

definition: A client-side script running in the background separate from web pages, intercepting network requests and handling offline caching.
example: The service worker implements a cache-first strategy to serve static web assets when users go offline.

definition: A background script execution thread allowing intensive computational work to run without blocking the main UI thread.
example: Offloading 3D mesh parsing to a dedicated Web Worker kept the user interface snappy and responsive.

definition: A security mechanism using HTTP headers that tells browsers whether a web application can access resources from another domain.
example: The API server returned a 403 error because our staging origin was missing from the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header.

definition: An HTTP response header layer that restricts which resources (scripts, styles, images) a browser is allowed to load.
example: A strict CSP prevents cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks by disallowing inline scripts and untrusted domains.

definition: A persistent, full-duplex communication protocol operating over a single TCP connection for low-latency data exchange.
example: We switched from HTTP polling to WebSockets to broadcast live cursor movements between collaborating designers.

definition: A low-level, client-side transactional database in modern browsers for storing significant amounts of structured data.
example: User drafts and large 3D scene files are saved locally into IndexedDB for persistent offline editing.

definition: A programming pattern that delays executing a function until a specified time has elapsed since the last time it was called.
example: Debouncing the search input handler to 300ms prevented unnecessary API queries on every individual keystroke.

definition: A technique that limits the rate at which a function is executed over a given duration, ensuring regular calls.
example: We throttled the window resize and scroll event listeners to fire at most once every 50 milliseconds.

definition: A set of HTML attributes that make web content and interactive applications accessible to assistive technologies.
example: Adding aria-expanded and role="dialog" ensured screen reader users can navigate custom modal overlays comfortably.

definition: A set of specific metrics standardized by Google (LCP, INP, CLS) to quantify real-world user experience on web pages.
example: Optimizing hero image compression improved our Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) score to under 2.5 seconds.

definition: A Core Web Vital metric measuring visual stability and unexpected geometric layout shifts during page loading.
example: Setting explicit width and height dimensions on responsive images lowered our CLS score from 0.28 to zero.

definition: A metric that measures overall page responsiveness to user clicks, taps, and keyboard interactions.
example: Refactoring heavy synchronous calculations out of click listeners helped our web app pass the 200ms INP threshold.

definition: Executing server-side compute logic in geographically distributed edge server locations closest to the end user.
example: Edge middleware inspects geographic headers and redirects users to regional subdomains in under 10 milliseconds.

definition: A visual diagnostic tool that creates an interactive treemap representation of package dependencies inside a JavaScript bundle.
example: Running webpack-bundle-analyzer revealed duplicate dependencies that had inadvertently leaked into vendor chunks.

definition: CSS media capabilities that apply styles based on the size of a parent container rather than the overall viewport width.
example: Using container queries enabled card widgets to adapt seamlessly between single-column and multi-column layouts.

definition: A binary instruction format for a stack-based virtual machine, executing native-speed code within web browsers.
example: We compiled our C++ physics engine to WebAssembly to achieve near-native simulation frame rates inside the browser.

definition: A modern web API providing low-level, high-performance hardware acceleration for 3D graphics and general-purpose GPU compute.
example: WebGPU offers significantly lower CPU driver overhead and superior compute shader capabilities than WebGL 2.0.

definition: A centralized pattern and library (e.g. Zustand, Redux) for managing global reactive data across decoupled components.
example: Zustand was selected for client-side state management because of its minimal footprint and subscription selector model.

definition: The process of taking a pre-trained model and further training it on a specialized, domain-specific dataset with backpropagation.
example: Fine-tuning a small open-weight LLM on our codebase allowed it to output idiomatic internal API calls consistently.

definition: High-dimensional vector representations of text, images, or audio that capture underlying semantic meaning and relationships.
example: Generating 1536-dimensional embeddings allows the search engine to match queries based on semantic intent rather than exact keywords.

definition: An architecture that retrieves relevant documents from an external knowledge base to augment an LLM prompt before generating answers.
example: Our RAG pipeline queries a vector database for clinical protocols before the model drafts recommendations.

definition: The practice of structuring, refining, and optimizing text prompts to guide AI models toward accurate and reliable outputs.
example: Adding negative constraints and strict schema instructions is a staple technique in production prompt engineering.

definition: A machine learning setup where a model performs a task without having received any prior explicit training examples for that task.
example: The foundation model classified clinical triage flags in a zero-shot setting with impressive accuracy.

definition: Providing a small number of input-output demonstrations inside the prompt to guide the model on formatting and logic.
example: Including three few-shot examples eliminated JSON formatting errors when parsing messy resume text.

definition: A prompting technique that encourages the model to generate intermediate reasoning steps before arriving at a final conclusion.
example: Enabling Chain-of-Thought reasoning dramatically improved the agent performance on multi-step mathematical calculations.

definition: A phenomenon where a generative AI model produces factually incorrect, misleading, or fabricated information with high confidence.
example: Grounded RAG architectures with strict source citations help eliminate model hallucinations in high-stakes domains.

definition: The maximum number of tokens (input plus output) an AI model can process and retain in memory during a single interaction.
example: A 128k token context window allowed us to pass entire codebase repositories into a single analysis request.

definition: The process of breaking down raw text strings into smaller numerical sub-word units or tokens for neural network ingestion.
example: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization splits rare technical words into common subword tokens.

definition: A specialized database engineered to store, index, and query high-dimensional vector embeddings using approximate nearest neighbor algorithms.
example: We deployed Pinecone as our vector database to perform sub-10ms semantic searches across millions of documents.

definition: A mathematical metric that measures the cosine of the angle between two multi-dimensional vectors to determine semantic closeness.
example: Cosine similarity scores above 0.85 indicate that two technical documents share strong contextual relevance.

definition: A hyperparameter that controls the randomness and creativity of generated text by scaling token logit probabilities.
example: We set temperature to 0.0 for deterministic JSON extraction and 0.7 for creative brainstorming tasks.

definition: A decoding strategy that chooses tokens only from the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches threshold P.
example: Setting top-p to 0.9 discards low-probability tail tokens while preserving natural conversational flow.

definition: Compressing model weights from high precision (e.g. 16-bit float) to lower precision (e.g. 4-bit or 8-bit integer) to save memory.
example: 4-bit quantization allowed running a 70B parameter model locally on consumer hardware with negligible quality loss.

definition: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that freezes base model weights and trains small low-rank adapter matrices.
example: Using LoRA reduced our fine-tuning VRAM requirements by 80% while matching full fine-tuning benchmark accuracy.

definition: Training machine learning models using reward models trained on human preferences to align AI behavior with human values.
example: RLHF alignment significantly decreased toxic outputs and made the model more helpful for end users.

definition: The capability of an LLM to generate structured arguments to invoke external APIs, tools, and databases autonomously.
example: The agent leveraged function calling to look up user calendar slots and query weather APIs in real time.

definition: A foundational directive provided to an AI model that establishes its overarching persona, behavioral boundaries, and output format.
example: The system prompt instructs the assistant to respond concisely using GitHub-flavored markdown without conversational filler.

definition: An autonomous execution cycle where an AI perceives state, plans actions, calls tools, inspects outputs, and iterates until completion.
example: The agentic loop automatically ran unit tests, identified compiler errors, and edited source code until the build passed.

definition: A neural network component that calculates dynamic weighting scores between all pairs of input tokens across sequence positions.
example: Self-attention allows the transformer to correlate pronouns with their correct antecedents across long paragraphs.

definition: A deep learning architecture relying on self-attention mechanisms rather than recurrence or convolutions to process sequential data.
example: The transformer architecture parallelizes sequence processing during training far more effectively than legacy RNNs.

definition: A statistical measurement of how well a probability model or language model predicts a sample of text (lower is better).
example: The language model achieved a perplexity score of 4.2 on the standardized technical validation dataset.

definition: A neural model that processes a query and document together to compute an accurate relevance score for reranking search results.
example: Passing the top-50 vector search candidates through a cross-encoder reranker boosted retrieval precision by 18%.

definition: Latency is the time taken to process a single request (or first token); Throughput is the number of tokens or requests processed per second.
example: Speculative decoding reduced time-to-first-token latency while boosting overall generation throughput.

definition: The degradation of machine learning model performance over time due to shifting real-world data distributions.
example: Continuous monitoring pipelines detect model drift by comparing production inference distributions with training baselines.

definition: Optimized runtime software (e.g. vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) designed to execute neural network models efficiently in production.
example: Deploying on vLLM enabled PagedAttention, allowing continuous batching and doubling our GPU serving capacity.

definition: Programmable safety layers and validation rules wrapped around AI inputs and outputs to prevent policy violations and data leakage.
example: Input guardrails sanitize user prompts for prompt injection attacks before sending them to the core LLM.

definition: Training a base foundation model on paired datasets of explicit human instructions and desired responses.
example: Instruction tuning transformed the autocomplete base model into an interactive dialog assistant capable of following complex rules.

definition: An AI model capable of understanding, processing, and generating multiple types of input modalities (text, images, audio, video).
example: We fed the architectural blueprint image directly into the multi-modal LLM to extract room dimensions.

definition: A technique where a large model summarizes long prompts or knowledge into smaller, specialized prompt prefixes or student weights.
example: Context distillation enabled us to encode hundred-page API references into dense system prompt instructions.

definition: Splitting text into chunks based on natural semantic boundaries and topic shifts rather than fixed character counts.
example: Semantic chunking preserved complete medical protocol definitions without splitting crucial dosage numbers across blocks.
